lesson.title: Count distinct things

lead.text: The till log has two questions hidden in it. One asks how many sales were rung up, and the answer is the length of the list. The other asks which kinds of bread were sold, and that answer is shorter, because several entries are repeats. To get it you cross off every entry that has appeared before.

A query can do the crossing off. Writing DISTINCT straight after SELECT removes repeated rows from the result, so each different value is listed once. In the shop's orders table the status column is a good place to see it. Six orders carry only two statuses, and the picture lists the column both ways.

afterFigure.text: SELECT DISTINCT status returns paid and pending once each, no matter how many orders carry them. The second query reads the same column and removes its repeats.

queries.label: Every status
queries.sql: SELECT status FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Each status once
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT status FROM orders ORDER BY status;

lead.text: Each entry in the till log is one sale.

In the orders table the customer_id column repeats, because one customer can place several orders, as the first lesson showed. Asking for that column plainly gives one entry per order. Asking for it with DISTINCT gives one entry per customer who has ordered. The orders themselves are still in the table, so DISTINCT shapes the result and leaves what is stored alone.
DISTINCT treats NULL like any other value: if a column holds several NULLs, they collapse into one NULL in the result. The picture does this with the amount column, which holds a NULL for order 106.

afterFigure.text: The second result is shorter than the first, and one of its rows is the NULL. DISTINCT removes repeats, and it doesn't remove unknowns. Asking about unknown values is a separate question, which comes up again below.

queries.label: Every amount
queries.sql: SELECT amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Each amount once
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT amount FROM orders ORDER BY amount;

lead.text: Several orders point at the same customer.

queries.label: Every reference
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, id;

queries.label: Distinct customers
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id;

lead.text: Now the SELECT list gets a second column. DISTINCT compares the listed columns together, and two result rows count as repeats only if they match in every one of them. A row with Desk and 80 is a repeat of another row with Desk and 80, but it is a different row from one with Desk and 20.

Take the status and amount columns of the orders. Several orders are paid for 80 or for 20, so the pairs collapse. Order 106 is pending with an unknown amount, and the pair is still a row of its own. The picture shows the plain pairs and then the distinct ones.

afterFigure.text: The more columns you list, the more rows can count as different. A single column can repeat all day, and adding a column that is different in every row, such as the id, makes every row unique. DISTINCT then removes nothing at all. So choose the columns by the question you are asking.

queries.label: Every pair
queries.sql: SELECT status, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Each pair once
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT status, amount FROM orders ORDER BY status, amount;

lead.text: The orders table gives every order an id that no other order shares.
DISTINCT works on the whole selected row. This time the row is a customer paired with a status.

queries.label: Item and status
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT item, status FROM orders ORDER BY item, status;

queries.label: Customer and status
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, status FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, status;

lead.text: Often you want how many different values there are, and not the list. COUNT does the counting, and COUNT(DISTINCT day) counts the different days on which orders were placed. In the picture it sits next to the same question asked for the status column.

Counting has its own rule about unknowns. COUNT(DISTINCT x) skips NULL, because an unknown value isn't one more kind of value. SELECT DISTINCT x keeps NULL as a row of its own, as the amount column showed a moment ago. So listing the distinct values of a column and counting them can differ by one when the column holds an unknown.

afterFigure.text: Listing the different values and counting them are two questions, and a query can ask either. Pick the one that matches what you want to know. A later lesson takes counting further, and starts with the problem of what to count when some values are unknown.

queries.label: Different days
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT day) AS different_days FROM orders;

queries.label: Different statuses
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT status) AS different_statuses FROM orders;

lead.text: The amount column holds 80, 20, 80, 40, 20 and NULL.

queries.label: Distinct amounts
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT amount FROM orders ORDER BY amount;

queries.label: Count known distinct amounts
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders;

lesson.orientation: Distinguish result rows, distinct values and distinct combinations of values.
lesson.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A bakery's till log for the day reads: bun, loaf, bun, roll, bun, bagel, loaf. Each entry is one sale, and the owner wants to know what the shop sold.

That is really two questions. One asks how many sales were rung up, and the answer is the length of the log. The other asks which kinds of bread sold at all, and its answer is shorter, because a bun appears three times and a loaf twice. To get it you go down the log and cross off every entry that has already appeared.

A query is in the same position. Sorting rows leaves them in a tidy order, and a sorted list can still repeat itself. This lesson shows how to ask for each different value once and how to count the different values. It also settles what 'different' means when a result has more than one column.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count different values and different combinations, and know what DISTINCT leaves alone.

recap.keyIdea: DISTINCT collapses result rows that match in every selected column. It changes the result only, so choose the columns you want to compare.

blocks.text: Back at the till log, seven sales became a shorter list of kinds. You counted 4 kinds of bread, then 3 customer ids and 5 customer and status pairs, and adding a column made more rows count as different.

recap.nextHook: Counting different values is one way to boil many rows down to one number. The next lesson turns to totals and averages, and begins with four pupils, one of whom didn't answer a survey, which raises the question of what to divide by.

questions.prompt: How many rows does SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders return?
hints: Collect the different customer ids.
Repeated references collapse into one result row.
Make a list of the customer ids with each one written once, then count that list.
questions.onCorrect: 3. DISTINCT keeps each customer id once, so repeated references collapse into one row.

misconceptions.feedback: That is every order. DISTINCT collapses repeated customer ids.

questions.prompt: In the orders table every order has its own id. Why does SELECT DISTINCT item, id still return every row?
hints: DISTINCT compares the entire selected row.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: DISTINCT compares the complete selected row. Even when item repeats, the unique id makes every item-and-id pair different.

questions.onCorrect: Each item and id pair is different. DISTINCT compares the whole row, and the ids differ.

misconceptions.feedback: DISTINCT works on text as on numbers. The columns you list decide the outcome.
Items repeat: Desk and Book appear more than once.

questions.prompt: The amount column of the orders holds 80, 20, 80, 40, 20 and NULL. What does COUNT(DISTINCT amount) return?
hints: Ignore missing values for this count.
Count the different known amounts, not the orders.
Write each known amount once, then count the entries in that list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The known distinct amounts are 20, 40 and 80. COUNT does not include NULL.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Only the known amounts 20, 40 and 80 count, each once.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the unknown amount as a value. COUNT(DISTINCT amount) skips it.
That counts every known amount, repeats included.

questions.prompt: How many rows does SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, status FROM orders return?
hints: List the statuses separately for each customer.
Compare the full two-column row.
Write each customer's statuses once, then count the different customer and status pairs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Customer 1 has paid; customer 2 has paid and pending; customer 3 has paid and pending. That makes five pairs.

questions.onCorrect: 5. DISTINCT compares the full customer and status pair, and customers 2 and 3 have both statuses.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts customers only. Status is part of the row too.
That counts every order. Some customer and status pairs repeat.

questions.prompt: A result column contains North, South, North and NULL. How many rows remain after SELECT DISTINCT?
hints: Remove repeated North only.
One NULL remains as a distinct result value.
The remaining values are North, South and NULL; count these result rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: North, South and NULL form three distinct result rows.

questions.onCorrect: 3. DISTINCT collapses the repeated North, and NULL stays as one result row.

misconceptions.feedback: NULL is not removed by DISTINCT. It stays as a result row.
North is repeated, so DISTINCT keeps it only once.

hints: SELECT reads; DISTINCT shapes its returned rows.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: DISTINCT removes duplicate selected rows from the query result. It does not delete rows from the stored table.

questions.onCorrect: Only the query result. DISTINCT shapes the rows returned and leaves the stored table alone.

misconceptions.feedback: DISTINCT reads the table and never alters it.
Keys belong to the table's definition. A query cannot change them.

questions.prompt: A bakery's till log for the day reads: bun, loaf, bun, roll, bun, bagel, loaf. How many different kinds of bread were sold?
hints: What counts as a repeat here?
Cross off a kind each time you meet it again.
List each kind once, then count that list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The kinds are bun, loaf, roll and bagel, so there are four.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Seven sales, but only four kinds. DISTINCT keeps each different value once.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every sale. The question asks for the different kinds.

questions.prompt: DISTINCT colour, size is applied to the rows (red, S), (red, M) and (red, S). Which rows come back?
hints: Which rows are exactly the same in both columns?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two (red, S) rows match completely and collapse into one. (red, M) differs in size and stays.

questions.onCorrect: DISTINCT compares the whole selected row, so only rows that match in every column collapse.

misconceptions.feedback: All three rows share the colour, but DISTINCT compares size as well.
Two rows match in both columns, and DISTINCT collapses exact repeats.

questions.prompt: The rows (A, x), (A, y), (B, x), (B, y) and (A, x) are selected. How many rows does SELECT DISTINCT return?
hints: Compare both columns together.
Which row appears more than once?
Remove the repeated row and count what is left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only (A, x) repeats. Removing the duplicate leaves four rows.

questions.onCorrect: 4. DISTINCT drops a row only when every column matches another row.

misconceptions.feedback: That keeps every row. One of them is an exact repeat.
That counts the first column only. DISTINCT compares the whole row.
